en: If by chance she bears a son,
Whoever says this or that,
Whoever feeds on filthy gossip,
Let us cut off his head with a sword
And utterly destroy
Every scrap of his property!
If someone suddenly babbles,
If the people should rave without warning,
Brand him a corrupter of the nation
And give him that name.
If there is some prattling wretch,
Seize him and gouge out his eyes.
Let us plunder much from him
And levy a heavy fine;
If some fool raves,
Drag him along the road
And hand him over to the executioners.
He had brought them before him,
And drawn them close to his side.
Speaking softly but firmly,
Champion Kyyaz began:
“There are seven chambers in the treasury.”
The Jediger’s brave Kyyaz
Opened the treasury doors.
Heavy bolts of silk brocade
And all manner of coins he lavishly
Scattered among the old women,
Yielding to their demands.
Bright gold and white silver—
Without making them ask, brave Kyyaz
Gave the accursed old women
Sacks filled with treasure.
What else could wretched Kyyaz do?
He did not cease his villainy:
He smeared poison on their edges
And prepared seven razors.
On each razor’s edge
Was poison fatal at a touch.
“If Aichürök bears a girl,
Wrap her in pure white,
And saying, ‘My khan, your wish is granted,’
Bring me the glad tidings!
It was a girl I desired;
If you fulfill my desire,
By your fathers’ graves, seven mothers,
I will grant whatever you ask.
If you truly believe my words
And truly serve me,
But she bears a son,
He will fall into servitude in the end,
And ultimately harbor an enemy’s hatred.
In the end he will do no good,
But bear immeasurable enmity.
If she bears a son,
Cut his umbilical cord with it,” he said.
The “razor steeped in poison”
Was given to the brood of the accursed,
The seven sorcerous old women.
Such was the nature of those crones:
They had reached ninety without dying,
And never suffered earthly torment.
They were witches like ogres,
And their people followed them into wickedness.
At the hands of the seven old women,
Many infants who might have grown
And come to be called children
Had died and vanished.
They were drunkards who meddled in disputes,
Greedy schemers who plundered the world.
The seven sorcerous old women
Were never satisfied, even in death;
Even with their heads beneath the earth,
They would not cease corrupting the people.
At every step they plotted,
And never abandoned their great wickedness.
People trembled at the sight of them;
Great spell-casters and enchanters,
All seven were nothing but calamity,
Practiced in uncanny arts.
They were the very eyes of seven corrupters,
Calamity itself.
Each was a true scourge.
Whenever a woman went into labor,
They would blindfold her,
And someone would take her child.
They gave no thought to its tender age,
Nor ever had a day when they feared God,
But simply killed it.
Once the people had gone, brave Kyyaz,
Showing them to no one
And letting no person know,
Led the seven sorcerous old women
To a place amid encircling plane trees,
Where brave Kyyaz’s golden throne stood:
To the palace of the golden throne,
Into brave Kyyaz’s fortress,
He brought the seven sorcerous old women.
“My cunning mothers, heed my words.
If her child is a boy,
Consider what manner of child he is:
His forebear set fire to grassy lands,
Planted his banner on tufted plains,
And raised an uproar across the earth.
His distant forefather was brave Manas,
Born after going to Altai,
Who shook the whole world,
A lion who led the nations.
He shot down twelve giants,
And became a torment in the heart
Of the Black Chinese and Manchus.
He took golden tribute from the khagan;
The vast, settled Chinese host,
As countless as black beetles,
Was left weeping by him.
Know well what I have told you.
I will give you many animals as gifts.
My dear seven mothers,
If you serve me well,
I will give you red-tailed camels
And lavish riches without stint.
I will make your yaks number ninety
And fill your homes with wealth;
Mothers, I will set your hearts at ease.
I will dress you in robes of red silk,
And make the hems of those robes
So broad that they sweep the ground.
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
I will make all my settled people
Know and honor you, my seven mothers!
If you should die unexpectedly,
If chance brings you an early death,
I will have a golden mausoleum built
And upon the crown of that tomb
Have an inscription carved in ruby.
I will make all who see it marvel
And spread your fame among the multitude.
From a spring beneath the bending hills
I obtained something that kills outright:
I had these razors made,
And upon their edges
Had dragon’s venom,
The vapor of a poison that kills without a sound,
Firmly fixed.
I had them wrapped in finery
And consecrated them
For bringing death to the child;
Half my livestock
I spent on these razors.
My seven mothers, dearer than anyone,
If Aichürök bears a son,
Be sure to cut his umbilical cord.
Secretly destroy the child
And put an end to him!
Show me your skill:
Find a way to touch
His navel with the razor,
Destroy him and scorch his mother’s heart;
Put an end to him.
Make the child vanish,
And if you set Kyyaz’s affairs right,
I will grant whatever you ask.
Seven mothers, I will give you
Red brocade measured by the foot!
I will never send you from my side
But keep you as my precious treasures.
Dear mother, I will take you
As my own mother!
Leave my concubine and take my wife;
Leave them both and take the one you choose.
For riding to feasts and celebrations,
For prancing wherever you go,
It is a fine and well-mannered beast:
Take my fleet bay racehorse.
Take all my abundant wealth,
Take every possession I own;
Know how precious this is to me.
I will not begrudge the least of my wealth.
“Keep watch over your seven aged mothers.
Let human eyes attend to us.
Gather together all the Jediger
Of Jeti-Özön,
And before my son Kyyaz—
So your seven mothers may be content—
For the sake of the one Creator God,
Know that the desire of poor old women
Like your seven mothers is for husbands.
Fulfill our yearning words:
Choose men of thirty,
Obtain your people’s consent,
Issue your command throughout your lands,
And wed us to them.
Gold is stone and stone is stone,
But our husbands will be more precious.
Let nothing stand between us; may these words
We have spoken come true.
If that wretched woman in labor
Bears a son,
We will contrive to steal him.
To that true realm of no return
We will send the child.
In our frenzy we will take her child;
Whether in jest or earnest,
We will suck his blood while he still lives,
And share in the blood
Of the champion destined to rise above the multitude.”
So spoke the seven old women,
Uttering monstrous words like ogres,
Proposing their scheme to brave Kyyaz
And speaking of terrible trouble
For Aichürök.
Saying, “So it shall be,”
And that everything was settled,
They made their pledge.
Before the seven fiends went
To Chürök in her labor,
Kyyaz said, “In Khan Kyyaz’s house
You shall carry firewood and pour water,
Water your horses tirelessly,
And make your names renowned among the people.
I shall set your hearts at ease among the nation
And make you queens, rulers among women.
My dear seven mothers,
Consent to what I have said
And grant what I desire.”
Thus brave Kyyaz
Spared none of his wealth.
To slaughter the child
Of the woman Aichürök,
He appointed the seven old women.
The seven corrupting crones
Agreed to his demand:
To remove the young child
From this world,
To fill his body with poison,
And receive gold from Kyyaz.
“My dear Kyyaz, we agree;
According to the meaning of your dream,
We shall undertake this deed.
We will serve
A precious man like you, my son.
We shall obey your words,
My son, and grant your wish.
We shall ease the pain that ails you
And open wide your dimmed eyes.
We shall bring back what you have lost
And banish your grief.
If we fail to do your bidding,
Cut off our heads with a sword;
Spare not the least breath of life,
But slaughter us all.
If we make that child disappear
And set Kyyaz’s affairs right,
Consent to whatever
Your seven aged mothers ask,
And grant us our desire.
This is our wish, Khan Kyyaz;
